state: Hey team! Saturday's the day — the Ridgeline Gravel Century is a go, all 102 miles of rolling farm roads and canyon climbs. Everyone's bikes are dialed in: fresh brake pads, tubeless tires topped off, and I double-checked that all twenty-two of us have helmets and mirrors. We'll roll out at 6am while it's still cool, which is smart because the forecast has the afternoon climbing to 101°F with almost no shade after mile 40. Here's the thing I want you all to really look at, though: our support van is only stopping at mile 20 and then again at mile 78, which means once you leave that first stop you're on your own for 58 miles with whatever's in your bottles. I know some of you like to travel light, but two bottles isn't going to cut it once that heat index climbs past 100 for three-plus hours in the saddle. I've asked the route captain twice about adding a stop around mile 50 and haven't heard back, so for now, plan on carrying at least four bottles or a bladder, and please, please eat your electrolyte tabs before you're thirsty, not after. Everything else about the day is honestly pretty chill — quiet roads, courteous drivers, gentle grades. It's really just that stretch in the heat with nothing to refill that's got me wanting everyone to plan ahead. See you at the start line!

- Heading to Cedar Bluff this weekend for some top-rope routes on the west face.
- Anchors are the two bolts we set last season; haven't had them checked by anyone since.
- Sarah's leading the outing, and she's only climbed outdoors twice before this.
- We've got one 60m rope and one set of runners between the four of us.
- Weather looks clear all day, so that part isn't a concern.

So funny story — my daughter finally learned to ride without training wheels last month, and now she wants to 'race' me every evening. We loop around the community park path, maybe three-quarters of a mile, totally flat and paved, with a fence separating it from the road the whole way. Helmet's non-negotiable, we go slow, and at the two street crossings we still stop and look both ways even though cars almost never come through. Honestly the most dramatic moment so far was her slamming the brakes to stare at a duck. It's turned into our favorite little ritual before dinner.

We finally got the site booked for next weekend and I am so ready to just get out of the house with the kids for two nights, though I'll admit I was scrolling through the campground map at midnight and realized our spot backs right up to the creek where the current picks up speed after that bend, and the bank there drops off pretty sharp instead of sloping in gradually like it does further down, and of course my two are going to want to wade in the second we get out of the car because that's just how they are, so I need to remember to actually pack the life vests instead of just tossing them in the garage pile like I did last time when we ended up not using them at all, and I still haven't figured out where the nearest ranger station is if something happens because cell service out there is spotty at best, my husband keeps saying we'll be fine because we always are, and I mostly believe him, but there's also that overlook trail nearby that the site description mentioned has some loose gravel switchbacks with no railing, and with three kids under eight running around while we're setting up the tent and trying to get the fire going, I know we won't be watching all of them every single second, so I really do need to sit down tonight and make an actual list of what we're bringing instead of throwing it together tomorrow morning like usual.

goin out to lake herron in the mornin for a swim, bouy to bouy is bout 1.2 miles. checked the water temp app last nite, said 41 degrees, kinda cold but figured id just push thru it, no wetsuit tho cuz mine ripped last month and havent replaced it yet. gonna go alone since everyone else bailed, phone stays in the car so no way to call if somethin goes wrong. shuold be fine i think, just gotta swim fast to stay warm lol.

The route we've booked for Thursday is a genuinely intimidating-looking wall — a sheer, forty-meter overhanging limestone face that our photos make look like something off a magazine cover — but the outing itself is about as controlled as climbing gets. Our guide is IFMGA-certified with fifteen years on this exact cliff, the anchors are permanent, redundant bolted stations inspected every spring, and every one of us will be on a top-rope she's already rigged and tested from above before we touch the rock. She's bringing an assistant to manage belays from the ground and run through harness checks twice before anyone leaves the ledge. It looks terrifying in the photos; in practice it's closer to a very scenic, very supervised afternoon.

Took the blue groomer down from the lodge today, the one everybody insists is 'basically a green trail wearing a costume.' Patrol had orange fencing around two icy patches near the tree line, which, fine, noted, I gave them a wide berth like a reasonable adult. Snow guns were still running section three so visibility dipped for about ten seconds, mildly dramatic, survived it. Wore the wrist guards my sister keeps nagging me about, mostly to make her happy. Nothing about today required a helmet-cam highlight reel, which is honestly the most exciting part.

We're taking the kids to Pelican Cove Saturday and I saw the lifeguard schedule only covers ten to two even though the tide charts show the strongest pull happening right around eleven when that rip current warning flag goes up most weekends, and my youngest still doesn't listen when I tell him not to go past the sandbar, so I'm going to have to basically not let go of his arm the entire time while also watching my older one who thinks he's a stronger swimmer than he actually is, and there's no way I can watch both of them every second if they split up, so I guess we're doing shifts, one parent in the water and one on the sand, no exceptions this time.

Okay so I have to tell you about Marcus's plan for Saturday because I still can't quite believe it — he wants to free solo the north face of Kestrel Ridge, that's the 300-foot route with zero bolts and that gnarly runout section near the top that even the guidebook calls 'committing.' No rope, no harness, no gear at all, just chalk and his shoes. I asked him three times if he meant top-roping and he just laughed and said 'where's the fun in a rope.' He's done the route before with protection, sure, but going up there with literally nothing to catch him if he slips on that crux move — one bad hold, one gust of wind at the wrong second, and there's no second chance, it's just a straight fall onto talus. I brought up that even world-class free soloists have died doing exactly this kind of thing and he just shrugged and said he trusts his hands. I'm going along to watch from the base but honestly I don't know what I'd even do if something went wrong up there, there's no cell reception for the first twenty minutes of the approach trail either. I keep hoping he'll bring the rack at the last minute but he's already told his roommate not to bother packing it. I love the guy but I really wish he'd let me talk him into at least a top-rope setup.

- Summit ridge hike, exposed above treeline for 2 miles
- Afternoon thunderstorms forecast, we're starting at noon
- No rain gear packed, just water bottles

Last summer when we went up to Cutter's Basin for the long weekend, I remember standing at the site going, huh, that's a lot of claw marks on that pine, and our neighbor two sites over mentioned offhand that a sow and two cubs had been spotted near the dumpster just two nights before we arrived, which, sure, fine, noted, except then it turned out our site didn't actually have one of those metal bear boxes like the ranger station website said all the sites would, just a regular picnic table, so we ended up keeping the cooler and the bag of trail mix and honestly half our groceries in the tent vestibule overnight because the car was already packed to the brim with the kids' sleeping bags and there wasn't room to shuffle things around in the dark, and my brother-in-law kept saying it'd be fine because bears mostly just want an easy meal and won't bother a tent if there's no obvious food smell, which I'm pretty sure is not actually how it works, but by the time we realized the mistake everyone was already half asleep and nobody wanted to get back up and hike the stuff over to the parking lot two hundred yards away in the dark. We got lucky and nothing happened, but I still think about those claw marks.

So the overnight low for Friday is supposedly 38°F, which around here triggers immediate panic among people who've clearly never actually checked what their gear is rated for. I checked. Our bags are rated to 15°F, the tent's a proper four-season model my dad's had since before I was born and apparently still doesn't leak, and the campsite is a hundred feet from the car if anyone decides they'd rather just sleep in the back seat like a coward, which, fair, no judgment. We're also not exactly roughing it in some backcountry sense — there's a paved road to the site, a ranger station a quarter mile away with actual cell signal, and a fire ring we're allowed to use since there's no burn ban this week. My cousin keeps texting me articles about hypothermia like we're about to summit somewhere at altitude in a blizzard, but 38 degrees with a 15-degree bag is what most people would call 'a slightly brisk night,' not an emergency. I packed an extra wool layer for the kids because I'm not a monster, and honestly the biggest risk of the whole trip is probably my uncle's cooking over that fire ring. We'll be fine. We'll be better than fine. We'll be smug about it, actually.

- Night fishing off the jetty rocks tonight, tide's coming in fast
- Coast guard flagged small craft warnings for 8-10 ft swells
- Going alone, no vest, waves already breaking over the rocks

I go for run on the ridge trail this afternoon, alone like always. The path there is narrow, maybe one shoe wide in some place, and right side go down very far to the rocks below. Today the sky in the west is getting dark grey already, but I still have maybe five more miles to finish the loop. My phone show no bars since the parking lot. I bring only small water bottle, no jacket, because morning was so warm.
Pre-dawn descent of the Kestrel Pass switchbacks — 14% average grade over 6 km — will proceed without headlamps or reflective vests, group riding two-abreast, target speed 45+ km/h in freezing fog.

Tomorrow's group ride crosses the Ashford Viaduct at km 34, a 1.8 km span with no windbreak and a narrow shoulder. Current forecast has sustained crosswinds of 24 mph with gusts to 35 mph from the northwest, roughly perpendicular to the roadway. At typical group speeds of 25-30 km/h, gusts in that range are enough to push a rider off line without warning, and the shoulder leaves little margin for correction. No route amendment has been issued and the crossing hasn't been mentioned in tomorrow's briefing.

We're heading to Miller's Pond after breakfast and it's honestly our easiest outing of the summer, the dock there is wide and railed on both sides so I don't stress about the boys wandering off, they've both got their life jackets cinched on before we even get out of the car because that's just the rule no matter how much they groan about it, the only slightly annoying part is the dock gets a little slick near the ramp when it's been raining like it was last night, but the marina put down those rubber traction mats years ago so honestly even that's a non-issue, we'll probably be home by lunch with nothing more dramatic than a tangled line or two.

Yes, it's a 300-foot multi-pitch route, very dramatic sounding, but it's also our third season climbing it with the same certified guide, same double-checked anchors, same radio check-ins every pitch. Somehow still less eventful than parallel parking downtown.

Sunday's outing is the Lodge Loop snowshoe trail, 3.2 km of groomed, flat terrain maintained twice weekly by the resort's grooming crew. Elevation gain over the full loop is 40 m, distributed across gentle, evenly graded sections with no drop-offs adjacent to the trail. The route stays within 800 m of the main lodge at every point, and trail markers are placed at approximately 150 m intervals, visible in both directions. Forecast for the outing window is -4°C with light winds under 8 km/h and full daylight throughout, well within the operating range for standard winter layering. Group size is capped at eight participants with one trained lodge staff member accompanying, who carries a radio with a direct line to the front desk. Snowshoe bindings will be fitted and checked at the trailhead before departure, and each participant is issued a trekking pole for balance on the packed surface. The trail crosses no open water, avalanche terrain, or roadways, and the return route retraces the outbound path exactly, eliminating any route-finding uncertainty. Rest benches are positioned at the 1 km and 2.2 km marks. Hot cocoa service resumes at the lodge immediately after the group's expected return time of 11:30 am. Given the groomed surface, marked route, mild conditions, and proximity to staffed facilities throughout, this is designed as an introductory outing suitable for first-time snowshoers, including children over the age of six accompanied by a guardian.

ok so paddle day at glassy lake tmrw w the group!! it's literally the calmest lake ever, like barely any current, but we're all wearing our pfds the whole time bc rule is rule lol. forecast says it might get a lil breezy in the afternoon (like 10mph max??) so we're just planning to head back before noon just in case, easy peasy. bringing snacks obviously. cannot waittt
Can't wait for our little nature walk Sunday — it's that flat half-mile paved loop by the botanical garden, stroller-friendly, benches everywhere, and we'll be back in time for brunch!

Same loop as always this morning, the paved path around Miller Park that connects right back to the parking lot near the rec center, I had my phone clipped to my arm band like usual and my neighbor Priya was running the opposite direction so we crossed paths twice and waved, the sun was already up by the time I started so it wasn't even that dim, and honestly the biggest event was stopping to retie my shoe by the duck pond, I was back home before the kids even finished their cereal.

So excited for the snowshoe outing tomorrow! We're doing the ridge connector trail this time instead of the usual loop, which does have one short icy section near the overlook, but our guide flagged it on the map and we're all bringing our microspikes just for that part. Otherwise it's mellow rolling terrain the whole way, and we're wrapping up well before the afternoon temperature drop. Bringing extra mittens because apparently I always forget how cold my hands get!

- Backcountry snowshoe route today, off the marked trail system
- Avalanche advisory is 'moderate,' we're staying on gentle slopes below treeline
- Neither of us packed a beacon, just in case

On paper, Thursday's outing sounds like the kind of thing that makes non-climbers nervous: a five-pitch alpine route up the east buttress, complete with an exposed knife-edge traverse partway up that photographs dramatically enough to have made our club's calendar twice. In practice, every pitch is bolted with modern hardware replaced last year, we're climbing with two guides who've done this exact route more than sixty times, everyone's on belay the entire way including across the traverse, and we're turning around at the first sign of the afternoon clouds that typically roll in around 2pm. It looks like an adventure movie; it runs like a well-rehearsed drill.

Paddling the marina channel this evening. Wearing PFDs, staying inside the no-wake zone, checked tide tables — slack tide at 6pm. Traffic from motorboats is the only real factor, so we're sticking close to the seawall.

- Backcountry camp tonight in the burn-scar canyon
- Flash flood watch issued for our exact drainage until midnight
- Setting up tents on the creek bed anyway, it's the flattest spot

Wading out into the tailwater below the dam tonight even though the generators are scheduled to release right at dusk, which means the water level and current both jump substantially with almost no warning beyond a distant siren.

me and jake doin the ridge trail today. startin late, like 1pm cuz we slept in. forcast said storms rollin in around 3, we seen it before, figured we'd just push thru. trail goes up above treeline for like 4 miles, no cover up there at all, just rock and scrub. summit's at 13,200ft, we're plannin to be up top right around 3, maybe 3:30 if we're slow. jake says lightnin never actually hits people, i told him thats not true but he just laughed. neither of us got a jacket packed, just windbreakers, figured it wouldnt matter since we'd be movin fast. no bail out point up there either, once your past the saddle its exposed the whole rest of the way to the top, cant just duck off the trail into trees or nothin. cell signal cuts out about mile 2 so if somethin happens up top we're kinda on our own til we get back down below the ridge line. we did check the trailhead board, it had one of them signs about turnin back if you hear thunder but honestly by the time you hear it your already up there. anyway packin light, just some snacks and a liter of water each, shuold be back by dark if the storm dont slow us down too much. probably fine, we been up worse.

Took my old cruiser down the riverside path again this morning, same route as every Tuesday, flat and paved the whole way, more squirrels than people out that early, back home before my coffee even got cold.

cuttin across the lake today instead of goin round, saves like 40 min. ice been formin for a few weeks now but nobody's actually checked the thickness this year, some guy at the gas station said it looked fine from the shore. goin solo, no poles to test it or nothin, just walkin straight out toward the far dock.

Rope's fraying pretty badly near the harness end, we noticed it this morning, but replacing it would mean driving forty minutes to the gear shop, so. We're climbing on it anyway. What's the worst that happens, right?

So we ended up picking the back trail instead of the main loop because Dana insisted it'd be prettier, which, fine, it was, but nobody mentioned it crosses that little creek drainage where the snow bridge always looks solid until you're standing on it, and we didn't have poles to test it like we usually do because they were still in the other car, and it's not like there's a ranger checking that trail this time of year either, so we just sort of eyeballed it and went one at a time, which in hindsight probably should've been the plan from the start, not the thing we figured out halfway across.

goin fishin at the pond behind grandpas house again, same spot i been goin since i was a kid. water's like three feet deep tops, folding chair right on the bank, cooler full of snacks. probably just sit there til lunch then head back, nothin ever happens out there, thats kinda the point.
shark advisory's up again at the point but we fish off the pier, dont matter to us. tide's comin in fast tho, and the walkway back floods at high tide if we don't leave in time.

We're taking the canoes out after soccer practice and I still haven't found the kids' life vests from last summer because they're buried somewhere in the garage behind the holiday bins, and the marina said the afternoon wind usually kicks up on that lake around 3pm which is exactly when we'd be heading back across the open section instead of hugging the shoreline like we probably should, and my husband keeps saying we'll just grab whatever vests are in the rental shed even if they don't fit great, which, I mean, better than nothing I guess, but I really wish I'd just packed our own like I meant to.

Sunday's hike is the Overlook Trail, four miles round trip, which the brochure describes as 'moderate' in the same breathless tone it uses for the gift shop's 'artisanal' trail mix. In reality it's a wide, well-maintained gravel path with a grand total of maybe 300 feet of elevation gain spread out so gradually you'll barely notice it happening. There is exactly one spot, around the halfway point, where the trail runs close enough to a small drop-off that the park service felt compelled to install a wooden railing, which, fine, I appreciate the effort, though I suspect the primary hazard there is tourists backing up for a selfie. Everyone in our group is bringing the standard stuff: real shoes, not the sandals my brother-in-law wore last time and then complained about for a week, plus water, and a paper trail map even though the cell signal is actually solid the whole way, so that's more of a superstition than a necessity. The ranger station sits right at the trailhead, which means if anyone twists an ankle on the one slightly rocky section near the creek crossing, help is a fifteen-minute walk away at most, not a rescue helicopter situation. Weather's calling for mild temperatures and zero chance of rain, which around here counts as a miracle. Honestly the biggest logistical challenge of the day will be finding parking, since apparently half the county has the same idea for a Sunday hike. We'll survive. Probably even enjoy ourselves, against my better judgment.
Took the little one down the bunny hill again today, same gentle slope as every Saturday, ski patrol practically parked at the bottom, hot chocolate waiting the second we're done.

okay so update on the ultra training run today because it got WILD lol. so the plan was the high ridge loop, like 18 miles, and I knew the forecast wasn't great but I've been dying to log the mileage before my race in 3 weeks so I just went for it anyway. by mile 9 I'm up on the exposed section, like fully above treeline, zero cover, and the sky just goes from fine to genuinely apocalyptic in like 15 minutes flat, thunder rolling in close enough that I'm not even counting seconds between the flash and the boom anymore bc there basically isn't a gap. and here's the thing, I didn't tell anyone my actual route today bc I changed it last minute from the lower loop, my phone's dead bc I forgot to charge it after yesterday's run, and there's literally no tree cover or bailout point for like 2 more miles either direction. I just kept running bc turning around felt just as exposed as pushing through, ended up basically sprinting the ridge section trying to outrun a literal thunderstorm which, in retrospect, extremely not the move. made it down fine this time but ngl my hands were shaking after and not from the cold. lesson learned I guess, gonna actually tell people my route from now on.

Sunday's session covers the groomed intermediate runs on the north face, primarily Cascade and Juniper, both machine-groomed overnight with corduroy conditions reported as of the 6am snow report. Base depth is 85 cm with a firm, consolidated base layer beneath 12 cm of fresh overnight snow, which the resort's avalanche and grooming team classify as stable for in-bounds terrain; no backcountry or sidecountry sections are on the itinerary. Two sections of the run have exposed ice patches near the tree line, both flagged with standard orange bamboo markers per resort protocol as of this morning's patrol sweep. Visibility is forecast at good to excellent, with cloud ceiling above 3,000 m and winds under 10 km/h at ridge level, meaning lift operations should run without weather holds. Each participant will carry a trail map and be briefed on the two flagged sections before departure from the base lodge. Ski patrol maintains active coverage on both runs throughout the operating day, with the nearest patrol hut roughly 400 m from the midpoint of Juniper. Equipment checks, including binding DIN settings appropriate to each skier's ability level, will be completed at the rental counter prior to boarding the lift. Given the groomed surface, marked hazards, active patrol presence, and stable snowpack conditions, this outing is calibrated for early-intermediate skiers, with one instructor accompanying the group for the full session.
It's really just a quick little run, five minutes tops — except it's the closed backside bowl under today's high avalanche warning, and I'm going alone, ducking the rope while patrol's on lunch.

Evening spin planned on the greenway tonight! Lights are charged since it'll be dusk by the time we finish, sticking to the paved path the whole way, nothing more thrilling than dodging the occasional jogger.

The campsite we've reserved for the long weekend sits at 1,140 feet of elevation in the foothills, which after some initial hand-wringing among the group chat turned out to be low enough that none of the altitude concerns anyone raised actually apply — that's barely higher than the parking lot at the trailhead we use every month. The overnight forecast has lows around 58°F both nights, comfortably within range for the standard three-season sleeping bags everyone already owns, no special gear needed. The one water crossing on the access trail, which sounds more dramatic in the campground description than it turns out to be, is a seasonal creek currently running at about 3 inches deep according to the ranger station's update from this morning, easily stepped across on the exposed rocks without even getting our boots wet. The site itself is 0.4 miles from the main parking area on a wide, well-graded gravel path, and there's a ranger station staffed daily from 8am to 6pm just past the trailhead. Cell coverage, somewhat unusually for this area, is full strength the entire way in, according to three different people who checked their phones on the drive up last weekend. We're bringing the usual gear, nothing beyond what we'd pack for any mild-weather weekend, and honestly the biggest planning question left on the group chat is whether to bring the folding chairs or the hammocks, which feels like the right kind of problem to have.
Can't wait for the canyon rim hike Saturday! Heads up though, the exposed switchback section has zero guardrail and gets loose gravel underfoot, so wear real boots, not sandals like last time!

Saturday session: beginner kayak clinic at Lake Verdon, 9am to noon. Water temperature 74°F, air temperature 78°F, no wind advisory in effect. Lake is spring-fed, average depth 4 feet across the entire cove where the clinic runs, maximum depth anywhere in the bounded area is 6 feet. Six participants, one certified instructor, one assistant on the dock. Each kayak stays within the marked swim-cove boundary, roped off with buoys 40 yards from shore. Personal flotation devices required and checked before launch; instructor confirms fit on each participant individually. No boat traffic permitted inside the buoy line per marina rules. Paddles are the stable, wide-hulled recreational type, not touring kayaks. Forecast shows clear skies through the afternoon, zero chance of precipitation, wind under 5 mph all day. Lifeguard stationed on the dock for the full session. Participants practice basic strokes, capsize recovery in three feet of water near the dock, and re-entry technique with the instructor spotting each attempt. Break for lunch at noon, gear returned to the rental shed, kayaks hosed down and racked. Marina staff log each participant in and out. Nearest parking lot is adjacent to the dock, thirty seconds' walk. Cell service is full strength throughout the cove. No prior kayaking experience required for this session; it's designed as an introduction. Session wraps by 12:30, well within the three-hour rental window.

Fishing off the reinforced, chest-high-railed pier at Cormorant Bay this evening, life vest on per marina policy — current picks up near the pilings after dark, so we're packing up well before dusk regardless.

Route: Foxglove Meadow Loop, 2.1 miles, gross elevation gain 140 ft on paved and hard-packed gravel surface with no sustained grade above 4%. Trailhead elevation is 610 ft, the trail is rated accessible-grade by the parks department, and it's mowed and inspected weekly. Forecast for the 10am departure is 68°F, clear, with wind at 3 mph; there are no water crossings or exposed sections, and cell coverage is continuous the entire way. Benches appear roughly every quarter mile, and the group of four should finish in about 45 minutes at a casual pace, well within daylight, with nothing beyond standard walking shoes required.

Tomorrow morning I swim again at the roped area of Lake Tomas, same place every week. Water is calm, no boats allowed there, and my friend Elena watch from beach chair like always while I do my slow laps.

Forecast flipped on us but we're still paddling out to Windham Point solo tonight, six miles offshore, storm cells rolling in by eight, and I left the PFDs drying in the garage again — should be fine, right?
same trail as tuesdays, told sara what loop im doin and when im back cuz phone signal drops past the second bridge, taped my ankle after tweakin it last week, back before the trail gates lock at dusk

Today's plan: three laps on the Harlow Peak backside trees, accessed via the unpatrolled gate past lift 4. This zone is inbounds but not part of the daily grooming or avalanche mitigation route; ski patrol sweeps it only on request, not on a fixed schedule. Snow report shows 18 cm of new snow over a wind-affected crust, with isolated rocks exposed near the ridge where coverage is thin. Two of us skiing together, no radios, relying on cell service which drops intermittently in the lower gully. Neither of us is carrying a beacon, shovel, or probe; this is inbounds terrain so the resort doesn't require it, though the trail map notes 'variable conditions, ski with caution' at this access gate. Visibility is good, winds calm, temperature 22°F. We checked the base area board, which lists this zone as open with no closures, but the last patrol note on the board is from two days ago. The terrain funnels into a narrow gully about two-thirds of the way down, maybe 15 feet wide at its pinch point, with exposed boulders on both sides where the snow has scoured thin. We plan to space out through that section and regroup at the bottom where it opens back onto the groomed run to the lodge. No lessons or instructor involved; both of us are intermediate-to-advanced skiers who've done this run a handful of times before, though not this season. First run starts at 10am.

took the avalanche safety course two winters ago so i know the drill, transceiver practice and all that, figured that counts for something today. patrol posted high avy danger this morning and closed the summit access gate, rope's up with the sign, but the traverse around the backside ridge into blackfin bowl isnt actually roped off, technically its just 'not recommended,' so i figured the course cert makes it fine to duck around and drop in anyway. going alone, told nobody where im headed cuz everyones busy today and i didnt wanna wait around. wind's been loading the lee side of that bowl since like 4am accordin to the weather station, cornice over the entrance looked bigger than last time i seen it, maybe 6 feet of overhang now. no beacon on me today tho, left my pack in the truck by accident and didnt wanna hike back up for it, figured one run cant hurt. visibility droppin in and out, cloud ceiling keeps swallowin the ridge line every ten minutes or so. the entry chute necks down to maybe 8 feet wide between two rock bands before it opens into the bowl proper, thats the part that always gets me a lil nervous ngl. no cell signal out there either, checked before i left the lot. figure ill just go fast and get thru the exposed part quick, thats basically a safety plan right. patrol wont even know im out there til im back at the lodge for lunch.

Route for tomorrow: Thistle Creek fire road, 6.2 km out-and-back, average grade 3%, surface is compacted gravel maintained by the county for vehicle access. Start time is 7:15am, with sunrise at 6:52am, so the entire run is in full daylight. I'm carrying 500 mL of water and a phone with GPS tracking shared to my training partner's app. Temperature at start is 58°F, rising to a forecast high of 71°F by 9am. The creek crossing at the 3 km mark is running high after this week's rain, so I'll use the fixed wooden footbridge rather than the usual stepping stones, which are submerged. Total elevation gain over the route is 95 m, spread evenly with no single steep pitch.
We shall pitch our tent a mere 0.2 miles from the car park, with the overnight low forecast at a mild 61 degrees and scarcely a breath of wind expected before our departure at nine tomorrow morning.
Tonight we paddle to the small island, is 4 kilometers across the open channel where big ships pass. Water is very cold now, but nobody wearing life jacket because we forget to bring them.
Rip current advisory's up at Crescent Bay and the lifeguard tower's empty for the season, but sure, let's do our usual mile swim out past the sandbar anyway, what's the worst that happens.

Heading back to Larkspur Cove for a swim before breakfast — it's the calm little inlet by the marina, lifeguard's already up in the chair, and Priya's coming along like every Sunday for our usual loop around the buoys.
Today we climb small cliff near river, only twelve meter high. Rock is little wet from rain yesterday so we use extra chalk and our friend Dmitri check every hold before we start, so is okay.

So excited for our camping trip tomorrow, it's going to be so nice to unplug for a couple days! The ranger mentioned there's been a raccoon or two getting into unlocked coolers lately, so we grabbed a proper bear box this year just in case, and we're keeping all the food sealed up overnight like they suggested. Other than that it's our usual spot by the lake, flat ground, easy walk from the car, nothing fancy. Can't wait, packing the marshmallows as we speak!

Tonight's ride includes about four hundred meters along Route 9 where there's no shoulder, so we're dropping into single file with blinking taillights on before we get there and regrouping once we're past it.

We plan to fish from the rocks beneath the old pier this evening; neither of us thought to check the tide tables beforehand, and the rocks nearest the water turn rather slick well before the tide is fully in.

- East face route again this weekend, 40 meters, three bolted pitches, same team as always
- Skipping helmets today since it's just top-roping and everyone forgot to grab them
- Anchors and ropes all inspected and fine, no concerns there
- Loose scree at the base where the trail approaches, a few slips already this season
